About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water.
About 97% of Earth's water is salty.
Most of Earth's fresh water is locked up in ice and glaciers.
Around three-quarters of the sea floor still hasn't been mapped in high detail.
The ocean produces a large share of the oxygen we breathe.
The Mid-Ocean Ridge is the longest mountain range on Earth, mostly underwater.
The deepest point in the ocean is deeper than Everest is tall.
Ocean water is salty partly because rivers carry dissolved minerals into the sea.
Tides are mostly caused by the Moon's gravity.
The Bay of Fundy in Canada has some of the highest tides in the world.
The Gulf Stream carries warm water across the Atlantic towards Europe.
Icebergs are made of fresh water.
Only about a tenth of an iceberg shows above the water.
Sea ice forms from frozen seawater.
Snowflakes usually have six sides.
No two snowflakes are believed to be exactly alike.
Snow is actually clear; it looks white because it scatters light.
The largest recorded snowflakes are said to have been 38 cm wide (Montana, 1887).
Fresh snow is mostly air, which makes it a good insulator.
Igloos can be much warmer inside than the air outside.
Hail forms when raindrops are carried up into freezing parts of storm clouds.
Lightning is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Lightning strikes Earth around 40–50 times every second.
Thunder is the sound of air expanding rapidly when heated by lightning.
You can estimate a storm's distance by counting between lightning and thunder.
Rainbows are full circles — the ground usually hides the bottom half.
A double rainbow's second arc has its colours reversed.
Clouds can weigh hundreds of tonnes.
Fog is a cloud that touches the ground.
Raindrops are shaped more like hamburger buns than teardrops.
Tornadoes are most common in the United States.
Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are the same kind of storm in different oceans.
Hurricanes spin anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere.
The eye of a hurricane is calm.
Earth's atmosphere is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen.
The sky is blue because air scatters blue light more than red.
Sunsets look red because sunlight passes through more atmosphere.
Auroras are caused by charged particles from the Sun hitting the atmosphere.
Auroras happen near both poles: aurora borealis in the north, australis in the south.
Earth's magnetic field has flipped many times in its history.
Earth's magnetic north pole wanders over time.
Earth's core is about as hot as the surface of the Sun.
Earth's inner core is solid metal, mostly iron and nickel.
Earth is not a perfect sphere; it bulges at the equator.
Earth's crust is broken into tectonic plates that slowly move.
Continents move about as fast as fingernails grow.
There was once a supercontinent called Pangaea.
Earthquakes happen thousands of times a day, mostly too small to feel.
The strongest earthquake ever recorded struck Chile in 1960.
The Ring of Fire around the Pacific has most of the world's volcanoes.
There are more volcanoes under the sea than on land.
Lava can be over 1,000 °C.
Volcanic ash is made of tiny bits of rock and glass.
The 1815 eruption of Tambora caused 'the year without a summer' in 1816.
Krakatoa's 1883 eruption was heard thousands of kilometres away.
Diamonds and graphite are both pure carbon.
Diamonds form deep in Earth's mantle under huge pressure.
Quartz is one of the most common minerals in Earth's crust.
Amber is fossilised tree resin and sometimes contains trapped insects.
Fossils are usually found in sedimentary rock.
Stalactites hang from cave ceilings; stalagmites grow up from the floor.
The largest known cave passage is in Hang Sơn Đoòng in Vietnam.
Sand on many beaches is mostly tiny bits of quartz.
Some beaches have pink sand made from bits of red shells and coral.
Black sand beaches form from volcanic rock.
Glaciers are rivers of ice that flow slowly downhill.
Glaciers can look blue because dense ice absorbs red light.
Permafrost is ground that stays frozen for at least two years in a row.
Absolute zero, −273.15 °C, is the lowest temperature possible.
Water expands when it freezes, which is why ice floats.
Water is densest at about 4 °C.
Hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold water — the Mpemba effect — but it's debated.
Salt lowers the freezing point of water, which is why it's spread on icy roads.
Deserts can be cold: the Gobi has freezing winters.
Only about a fifth of the Sahara is covered in sand dunes.
Earth is about 4.5 billion years old.
Earth travels around the Sun at about 107,000 km/h.
A year on Earth is about 365.25 days, which is why we have leap years.
Seasons happen because Earth's axis is tilted, not because of its distance from the Sun.
Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January.
